newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: cricket - Dream start for new skipper Fleming.
newsitem.headline: cricket - Dream start for new skipper Fleming.

text.p: DUNEDIN, March 11 - Stephen Fleming had a dream beginning to his fulltime captaincy reign when New Zealand demolished Sri Lanka by an innings and 36 runs in the first test at Carisbrook.

The match finished with more than three sessions to spare when Sri Lanka, bolstered by a blistering century from wicketkeeper Romesh Kaluwitharana, ended their second innings resistance on 328 late on Monday afternoon.
For Fleming, who last week replaced Lee Germon as skipper, immediate success in the hot seat meant a gentle introduction to the rigours and demands of leading his country.
"Because it went so well and it ran my way, the honeymoon was great," the 23-year-old Canterbury player said.
But Fleming is experienced enough to appreciate tougher times may lie in wait during his captaincy tenure.
"One does think there are harder days down the track but I'm not going to think about them because that's a bad statement.
"It's just hard to believe it has gone so well."

Sri Lanka started the fourth day on 37 without loss, a long way from the 327 runs they needed to force the home side to bat a second time after New Zealand scored an imposing 586 for seven declared in their first innings before rolling the tourists for
222 first time around.
The Sri Lankan resistance to a persistent Kiwi bowling attack was initially minimal despite a pleasant 50 from opener Sanath Jayasuriya.

He and three of his colleagues were back in the pavilion at lunch when Sri Lanka were reduced to 102 for four and the early afternoon departures of Arjuna Ranatunga and Hashan Tillekaratne saw the tourists slump further at 133 for six.

Fleming later said his side lost some patience as Kaluwitharana, who belted a sublime 103 from an identical number of deliveries, and Chaminda Vaas, who finished with a test-best 57, racked up 137 for the seventh wicket at frenetic pace.
It wasn't until Kaluwitharana, a clean and bold striker of the ball, offered left arm spinner Daniel Vettori a return catch, that the Kiwis regained control of the situation.

Pramodya Wickremasinghe, who hit out for 43 in the first innings, was removed nine balls later and Vaas's departure after the addition of 14 runs, meant New Zealand were one wicket -- potentially one delivery -- away from achieving just their
seventh victory by an innings margin in test history.
Tailender Muttiah Muralitharan then showed a lot of spunk to spank 26 off 14 balls before he offered a lobbed return catch, and the third wicket of the innings for Simon Doull.

Doull finished with eight wickets in the match to lift his haul for the season from six tests to 27, and Fleming was in the luxurious position of looking back on a performance where virtually nothing went wrong for his side from the moment he lost the toss last Friday.
Sent in by Ranatunga, the Kiwis racked up their second biggest score in the test arena, and preyed on the tendency of the Sri Lankan batsmen to try to hit the leather off the ball.

Sri Lankan coach Bruce Yardley, while bemoaning his specialist batsmen's penchant to self destruct, traced his team's loss back to the first day when New Zealand survived a seaming track to reach 343 for four.
"We did some basic things wrong," Yardley said.

"Everyone knows we came into this game cold (after only two days of cricket on tour) but the players did not switch on from the first ball and it stayed like that through until the last ball on the first day.
"In test cricket you can't bowl on two sides of the wicket and get away with it."

The New Zealand side have suffered some wild swings in fortune this season, a first-up win against Pakistan in Lahore being followed by heavy losses in Rawalpindi and then to England in Wellington and Christchurch.

No one can have more enjoyed the return to the winner's lounge yesterday than coach Steve Rixon, who came under intense pressure as the side's form slipped and his input to the dumping was Germon was questioned.
"It was enormously satisfying mainly because it followed our improved performances in the latter couple of matches in the one-day series against England," Rixon said.
"Everything we did was organised beforehand and we implemented it.
"The formula for success isn't really that hard at international level.
"For the first time we implemented the basics, Sri Lanka were underdone and away we went."
